newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: U.S. sees good chance for Slovenia in NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees good chance for Slovenia in NATO.

text.p: The United States on Saturday told Slovenian leaders disappointed at their country's exclusion from the first round of NATO expansion that there was "no stronger candidate" than Slovenia for the second round.

"What I've explained to the president and the prime minister and the foreign minister (is) that while there are no guarantees, there is no stronger candidate than Slovenia for the next round," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said.

A NATO summit in Madrid on Tuesday invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to become the first ex-communist countries to apply for membership, despite pressure from France and others to include Romania and Slovenia as well.

The summit communique mentioned Bucharest and Ljubljana as promising future candidates, but Albright's comments on Saturday were the strongest suggestion so far that Slovenia, a former Yugoslav republic, would get in next time.

Following the summit, Albright, President Bill Clinton and Defence Secretary William Cohen have been visiting Central and East European states to explain the Madrid decision, which was taken under U.S. pressure.

After talks with Slovenian President Milan Kucan and Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, Albright told a news conference that in order to be sure of membership, Slovenia must continue its present course of democratic and economic reforms.
Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler told the news conference his country "in a way was disappointed that it was not admitted in the first round" but accepted Albright's assurances.

Slovenia and Croatia headed the drive to break up the former Yugoslavia by declaring independence in 1991, but unlike Croatia, Slovenia, an Alpine state of less than two million people, managed to stay out of the ensuing Balkan conflict.

Albright said that what NATO was looking for from Slovenia was a more bipartisan foreign policy, further economic reforms to encourage foreign investment and modernisation of its armed forces and a greater role in regional peace-keeping.
Despite its attraction to NATO strategists as a land bridge between Italy and Hungary, Slovenia has not yet restructured its armed forces from being a territorial defence backup to the Yugoslav army.
Its professional forces currently stand at only 4,100 although conscripts swell the number to some 56,000.
Thaler said his government felt the armed forces were "the proper size" but was working to modernise them.
President Kucan told a separate news conference later that Slovenia would press ahead with efforts to be included in Western institutions.

"The main task of Slovenia is to continue to work in the direction of reforms in order to qualify as a serious NATO candidate and to be included in the first round of members of the European Union," he said.
